subtopic: NATIONAL, WAR LABOUR BOARD
NATIONAL, WAR LABOUR BOARD
speechtext:
(a)	How many cases concerning wage increases or bonus payments have been before the national war labour board to date; (b) how many of these were brought before the board through applications by employers and how many through applications by employees; (c) how many wage increases have been granted by the board on employers' applications and how many on applications filed by employees; (d) how many bonus payments or increases have been granted to each of the two groups of applications; (e) what in each case were the grounds for granting the applications and what were the grounds for refusal in those cases where the application was rejected?
Mr. MITCHELL; (a) From the establishment of the National War Labour Board to May 6, 1942, one hundred and fifty-two applications have been received. Findings have been made in ninety-six cases, of which seventy-five had relation to wage increases or cost of living bonuses.
(b)	Of the seventy-five applications dealt with, fifty-three were initiated by employers, ten by employees and twelve were made jointly by employer and employee representatives. Of these applications, sixty-three had relation to wage increases and twelve to cost of living bonuses.
(c)	Wage increases, in whole or in part, were granted in forty applications filed by employers, in nine applications originating with employees and in twelve cases in which joint applications were made. In one employer and one employee application in connection with wage changes, application was refused.
(d)	Cost of living bonus payments or adjustments were authorized in ten applications originating with employers. In one application for relief from payment of additional bonus, the application was granted under the provisions of section 13 of the order. In one application by employer to adjust bonuses, permission was refused.
(e)	In twenty-six applications filed by employers, in one by employees and in seven jointly made, wage increases were approved under the terms of clause 11 (2) of the wartime wages and cost of living bonus order, as existing wages were found to be low compared with wage rates generally prevailing for similar work in like localities.
In two applications by employees wages were found to be low, and the board ordered an increase in some occupational classifications and wages were found to be not low in other classifications.
In two applications by employees wage increases were granted in part but not in full in order to bring basic rates into conformity with rates generally prevailing for similar work in like localities.
In one employee application an increase in basic wage rate was refused by reason of the fact that existing rates were not low within the meaning of the order.
In one application filed by employer proposed changes in salesmen's compensation plan was refused, the proposal being regarded as being in contravention of the provisions of the order.
In fourteen applications (with the concurrence on behalf of employees affected in cases where collective agreements were in effect), wage increases were approved in order that basic wages to employees in Canada might conform with rates being paid by the applicant companies to employees in comparable employment outside of Canada under collective agreements or by established practice. In all such cases it was stipulated that cost of living bonuses would not be paid.
In five applications by employers overtime payments were approved when employees were required to work more than the number of hours constituting a normal week's assignment.
In one joint application a wage increase was approved to take the place of piece work rates.
In one employer application a range of wage rates submitted was approved as not being excessive and having been in effect prior to the date of the order.
In one employer application standardization of basic wage rates was approved for air pilots employed in pooled operations.
Questions

In one joint application, following a collective agreement, permission was given to apply a bonus on an equivalent hourly rate basis, exclusive of overtime.
In ten applications originating with employers, payments of cost of living bonuses were approved on the ground that such payments would be "fair and reasonable" under the provisions of section 12 (b) of P.C. 8253.
In one application by an employer to be relieved of payment of additional cost of living bonus the application was granted on the basis of submissions that the undertaking in question was being conducted at a financial loss.
In one employer application for permission to make adjustments in cost of living bonus, the application was refused because proposed adjustments were inconsistent with the terms of the order.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SINKING OF SECOND SHIP IN ST. LAWRENCE
speechtext:
May I ask the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services whether the rumour is true that another ship has been sunk in the St. Lawrence?
Hon. ANGUS L. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services): Mr. Speaker, I had intended to make a statement on that matter and rose for that purpose, but yielded the floor to my hon. friend.
Yesterday I gave a statement to the press declaring that a freighter had been sunk in the St, Lawrence river by an enemy submarine. That statement was completely accurate according to the information at that time in my possession or in the possession of the department. I also stated that it would not be the policy to make an announcement of any future sinkings in this area, in order that information of value to the enemy may be withheld from him. That is the policy I must pursue. But inasmuch as the whole event really constitutes one inndpnt, I think
Shipping Losses

I should tell the house that another ship was sunk in the same general locality, at about the same time. While in future I must stand by the statement made yesterday, that we are not going to give information to the enemy which may be of assistance to him, nevertheless, these ships having been sunk in about the same wrnters and at about the same time, I think I can regard it as one incident and not come within the scope of the prohibition which I laid upon myself yesterday.
Information such as this cannot and will not be given in answer to questions in the house or elsewhere, and in no circumstances will it be given unless we are satisfied that the enemy will not benefit therefrom. To hon. members who are inclined to be critical of the censorship regulations and the silence that is observed with regard to these matters, I may say that German broadcasts are heard in the department, and this morning the German radio announced with great glee that a ship had been sunk in the St. Lawrence by one of their submarines; that this was the greatest distance from home their submarines had ever operated; that the whole thing had produced tremendous consternation in Canada; that the department had declared that no further announcements would be made; that this was an indication of our consternation, and generally they played the news up to the utmost degree. It is obvious that if they attach such importance to the matter, we also should attach similar importance to it, and we cannot dash around, giving out information which may in any way endanger the safety and lives of our men or the safety of our own or allied property, for the sake of gratifying any group of people, no matter how important they may be. But I think I should say that, while we had not the knowledge at the time the announcement was made yesterday, a second ship has been sunk.

speechtext: I want to thank the minister for the courtesy he has shown, which is in keeping with the manner in which he is administering his department.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yesterday I asked the minister whether the Royal Air Force stations were included in the commonwealth air training scheme. He advised me that they were not. A little later he said that the Royal Canadian Air Force had a sort of general control over the Royal Air Force schools. I also asked him then if the Royal Canadian Air Force posted men to these Royal Air Force centres. He advised me that they did. He went on to say that sometimes Royal Air Force men were posted to Royal Canadian Air Force schools. In view of the statement the minister has made that he has a kind of control over these Royal Air Force schools I think he should make a statement indicating clearly what the control is. When he has answered that question, I should like him to state how the difference in pay is made up if men from the Royal Air Force schools are stationed at Royal Canadian Air Force schools, and vice versa. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

With respect to control by the Royal Canadian Air Force over the Royal Air Force, we have a control with respect to both discipline and command. I must admit that at the present it is somewhat nebulous. I expect that as a result of the conferences which are to be held in the near future that situation will be clarified.
With respect to pay, I am very glad that that matter has been brought to my attention, because for months it has been stated in the press and on the public platform that the Royal Air Force schools received rations different from those of the Royal Canadian Air Force, and that as a result they are obtaining a lower standard of rations. Men of the Royal Air Force whose pay was lower than that of the Royal Canadian Air Force, according to the story, were having a very hard time to make both ends meet. The true story is that the Royal Air Force, wherever they may be in Canada, receive exactly the same rations as the Royal Canadian Air Force from the army service corps. That is number one. Number two is that their men receive the same pay as the Royal Canadian Air Force, with the exception perhaps of certain trades. Some trades are graded higher in the Royal Air Force than in the Royal Canadian Air Force, but that is a difference of administration by the different forces. But the standard or basic rate of pay

of the Royal Air Force is brought up to that of the Royal Canadian Air Force when the men come to Canada.

I come from a city and district that have given almost one-third or one-fourth of the cadets to the dominion, and naturally I want to ask one or two questions in regard to cadet services. There was a return to an order of the house in connection with cadet services in the air force. A lot of trouble is caused by having outside organizations of a private nature engaged in this work. They have done good work, I admit, but I object to having the whole policy of Canada upset in connection with the cadet services, which we have had from the days of confederation.
Take this particular branch of the department. An order was given, which will be
found in Votes and Proceedings, order No. 9, February, 1942, with regard to this particular cadet services department, in which it was shown that a private organization had been given rights and privileges, formerly the functions of school boards, in this matter. Apart from a few subscriptions, the department is paying for 7,000 cadets going to camp, and when the country pays for them it should have some control over the matter. This league is getting a grant of $25,000 a year, and it is going into the schools, some for the army, some for the navy and some for the air force. Toronto is spending $12,000,000 in connection with maintenance charges for

schools, and I suggest that the school boards and teachers should have some control and be consulted first. There are many men who served in the great war -and some who are in this war, who are teachers in the public schools and high schools, and in the separate schools as well. In the constituency of York South represented by my hon. friend (Mr. Noseworthy), there is a large collegiate, Vaughan road. Now you will have rival organizations, one for the army, one for the navy and one for the air force all in the schools and interfering with studies, using this private medium. I am not opposed to them, but they should be coordinated. They have done a lot of good work and I freely admit, as the minister said last night, that they are public-spirited citizens. I suggest, however, that there should be some coordination. The minister has put in a good deal of hard work on this question and he knows more about it than I do. I am one of those who appreciate what he has done and the league so far. He commanded a Toronto unit in the last war and is much respected there. The provincial minister of education at Toronto has stated that they want to train 50,000 cadets in Ontario at the expense of the municipalities and the schools of the province. I should like to find out what authority they have for that from this government and how this will affect the air league. Have they received requests from the army, navy or air department or from other departments of the government to do this, and why? What is the scheme? Does it not also supersede and interfere with the cadet league system? There are a great many of my own personal friends, whom I have known for many years, splendid patriotic citizens, who belong to the league.
I know most of them. They are public-spirited, and I think something should be done to explain the situation in view of Ontario's entry into it. They have an air league secretary in Ottawa who issues communiques almost daily, but I do not know what is being done. He has a new flag and has obtained the royal assent for it, by what authority I do not know, with parliament in session. My hon. friend the member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) is one of those who have been behind protecting strongly the flag which shelters us, and while perhaps matters of this kind should not, in time of war, be mentioned, I think attention should be drawn to this situation. I am glad that the hon. member for Davenport is aware of the change of flag proposed.

Mr. MaoNICOL: I am always aware of what is going on.

I know, but he may find the new flag over us before the league gets through. Thejr have plenty of leagues in this country. Who authorized the changing of the flag of the air cadets without the knowledge of parliament? How many of these separate flags have already been introduced in Canada's forces. I am not objecting, but under what authority? What sums of money does this league get?-$25,000 I understand. For what purpose do they get it, and who are the officers? They are using public property, school buildings, for drills and meetings, and there are not enough schools to go around for all this war cadet service. The minister who has been interested in education for many years, will appreciate that I am not objecting to the work of the league, there are many good people in it, but there should be some cooperation, and surely when parliament is meeting they should not be doing this without control. On what grounds of public policy were these services taken out of the control of school boards and boards of education in Canada, which have had control in the past? And do not forget, it was done without the authority of parliament, and is different from the navy and the army.
In view of the great record which the minister's department has made, for it has made a great record in an empire sense, I urge that he look a little further into it and get some control over it.
As to the summer air and other cadet camps, they are going to interfere with the migration of cadets to farms and with everyone who wants to be a farmer. The cry used to be, "I did not raise my boy to be a farmer but I raised him to be a hockey player", but since the war came all that is changed now. In view of the attempt to get the high school boys out on the farms there will be some interference with the league work. The minister used to be a star hockey and lacrosse player himself, I remember, and he was a great player who could give and take with the best of them. He should look into the whole situation. I was talking to the head of one of the largest collegiates in the dominion last week, and he said from a quarter to one-third of the students are now on the way to the farms. They used to go for four or five weeks, but now it is extended to eight or nine weeks. If we keep on, every one will want to be a doctor of agriculture; we are going to turn the city men instead of into doctors of law into doctors of agriculture, and make our collegiates agricultural

War Appropriation-Air Services
colleges in cities. If we have no control over some of these things we might as well go home. Since the dollar-a-year men have got control, all the affairs of the country are under their control and that of the bureaucratic boards. It seems to me that the cabinet and parliament are compelled to do goosestepping to these dollar-a-year men who pass conscription orders without the knowledge and consent of parliament. The country is controlled by a bureaucracy. I do not seek to interfere with the thousands who want to go on the farms. I am glad the schools are helping, because it is primary. I am not a farmer myself, but I have just as much knowledge of farming as some hon. members who pose as farmers, although I do not remember whether there are fifty-six or sixty pounds to a bushel of buckwheat, barley or timothy seed. I have seen many farms five and ten miles out of Toronto on the highways where the city and the province spent a good deal of money on roads and to furnish cheap light and power and transportation, but the farms are now deserted and untilled, and many are vacant.
But I hope the minister will look into the powers and functions of this league and other private organizations. During the last war when I was one of the heads of the city of Toronto, we had the air force cadets there and they did a tremendous work. Over 16,000 were trained as R.A.F. cadets and mechanics.
I hope some consideration will be given at the conference next week to the representations made last night by the hon. members for Brantford City, Lambton West, Lake Centre and others, and that the question of air force regiments will be taken up. They are in their infancy in England, they cooperate with the army and the navy; they are badly needed in this country, the territory of which stretches from ocean to ocean. One of the main reasons why some of these regiments should be formed is to guard the proposed new aerodromes and the camps and cooperate with the army and navy and the land and ocean services. Notwithstanding the lecture of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services to the municipalities last night, I can tell him that the municipalities of Canada have done more than those in any dominion of the empire in the way of giving to the government buildings and grounds free until they have no room for any expansion of their ordinary municipal utilities, and the universities also. Look at what Toronto di 1 in the last war and in this war to help cooperate, even to closing its annual fair, which helped in war to keep up morale.

I wish to ask some questions of the minister along the lines of those I asked last year. When a man joins the Canadian army he does so as a Canadian soldier; he goes overseas as a Canadian soldier to operate under the Canadian army which in turn is attached to the Canadian corps. The same is true of a man who joins the Royal Canadian Navy; he goes over in a Canadian ship, and although his unit may be cooperating with a British squadron, nevertheless he is operating under Canadian officers and the Canadian general staff. But in the air force a man joins the Royal Canadian Air Force; he goes overseas, and it is understandable why in the early stages, when there were not many of them, they were scattered through the Royal Air Force. The minister said last year that an attempt was being made to set up a Canadian squadron. I think he said yesterday that some twenty-two of these all-Canadian squadrons have been set up. But are the government and his department moving toward setting up the Royal Canadian Air Force as a separate entity overseas operating under its own general staff? It seems to me we ought to be moving in that direction for two reasons. One is that I think the men would prefer it. That is no reflection on the Royal Air Force, but it is the same matter of principle that was fought out in the last war. Those who have read Sir Robert Borden's memoirs will remember that it was proposed that Canadian units should be dispersed throughout the British armies and operate under British commanders; but the Canadians were adamant on that issue, insisting that Canadians should operate as a Canadian army, and I think that stand was amply vindicated. The operation of that Canadian corps forms one of the proudest pages in our history. Has the time not come now to form a Royal Canadian Air Force overseas under a general staff responsible to the minister here?
Another reason why that ought to be done is because of the matter I mentioned when the army estimates were up. That is, since the Canadian corps has been formed under General McNaughton, there must be an increasing attempt to allocate to the army corps sufficient air power to sustain it when it goes into action. One of the most tragic pages in British history has been written in the last few days. Hon. members will have read the reports from correspondents in Burma telling how some of the finest units in the British and Indian armies have been cut to ribbons for lack of air support; a pitiful story of men who for three months fought a rearguard action, bombed and machine-gunned from the air with practically no air support. We are not in a position to say where the fault lay or what could have been done about

War Appropriation-Air Services
the matter, but the people of Canada will never forgive this government or those responsible if Canadian troops have to go into action on the continent without adequate aerial support, and they certainly would'prefer that that aerial support should come from the Royal Canadian Air Force. The air force is no longer, as I understand, merely a bombing or fighting or interceptor force, it is a great deal more.
In modern war the air force has become, in some respects, the artillery of a mobile army. It is used to break up strong points of resistance. By dive bombing it is used to break up enemy troop concentrations, as well as for reconnaissance, and in conjunction with artillery being directed by the divisional commander on the ground. There will have to be the closest cooperation with and the best possible support of the Canadian corps by an air force, and preferably the Royal Canadian Air Force, when they go into action on the European continent. If this is to be done, it can be done only if there has been constant cooperation, coordination and) practice between the different forces.
It seems to me it is not sufficient in modern war for appreciations of situations to be made and operational orders to be issued to the different services, and then to try to work them out on paper. There will have to be constant cooperation between land and air forces, and that can be done only if the Royal Canadian Air Force is operating under or in very close conjunction with the Canadian corps. I should like to see the Royal Canadian Air Force, with its own general staff, operating with General McNaughton's general staff of the Canadian Army Corps. It may not be possible to do that right away. It may be that the taking of Canadians out of different squadrons of the Royal Air Force would upset the set-up over there, and therefore it cannot be done too quickly or suddenly. But certainly it will have to be done some time, and I would ask the minister if he and his officers are moving toward that goal. I would ask him if there is any possibility at the conference to be held next week of his discussing with British air officials the possibility of setting up the Royal Canadian Air Force under a separate command in Great Britain, and working in close conjunction with General McNaughton and the Canadian corps.

greater sense of frustration than in my attempts to Canadianize the Royal Canadian Air Force overseas. I might explain that under the joint commonwealth training scheme the scheme was to train individual pilots for the Royal Air Force. In that connection I shall read section 14 and following under the heading "Training for R.C.A.F. merged with joint training":
14. It is agreed that the government of Canada may, out of the Canadian pupils who complete their training under this scheme, fill vacancies which occur in the home defence squadrons of the Royal Canadian Air Force.
That is, fill vacancies out of the graduates, in Canada.
All the other pupils, on completion of their training, will be placed at the disposal of the government of the United Kingdom-
Then there is the saving clause, added by the government of Canada:
-subject to that government's making the arrangements indicated in article 15 and bearing liability, as provided for in articles 16 and 17 of this agreement.
Then there is the clause which to some extent protects the Canadian character of the pupils:
The United Kingdom government undertakes that pupils of Canada, Australia and New Zealand shall, after training is completed, be identified with their respective dominions either by the method of organizing dominion units and formations, or in some other way, such methods to be agreed upon with the respective dominion governments concerned. The United Kingdom government will initiate inter-governmental discussions to this end.
Then follows article 16, to which reference is made; and article 17 deals with pay and allowances, and has nothing to do with the matter under discussion,
As a result of the sentiments my hon. friend has so well expresed the dominion government took up with the government of the United Kingdom a year ago last January, through my colleague the Minister of National Defence who was then in Great Britain, the question of identifying Canadians by the creation of a certain number of Canadian squadrons. That was only so far so good, because there were too many of our pilots to fit into only twenty-five Canadian squadrons. However, it was at least a start.
Unfortunately-and I am saying this without blaming anybody-there was not always the same enthusiasm, if I may put it in that way, on the part of the air ministry, and particularly on the part of the officers of the Royal Air Force, for the Canadianization of our squadrons.

Perhaps it would go beyond that. There was some resistance both on the part of the senior officers of the Royal Air Force-though I must say that eventually, after my visit last summer, the air ministry came around to what I call the Canadian point of view-and among the officers of our own Royal Canadian Air Force. Therefore, even the Canadianization of our twenty-five squadrons has been somewhat difficult, although we have all the men required to fill them-and many times more than enough.
Even to-day some of those squadrons contain only 30 per cent or 40 per cent of Canadians. Of course some have gone up as high as 80 per cent and 90 per cent, and there was the squadron I mentioned last night with 98 per cent. Another complaint-perhaps I should not say it was a complaint- another representation which I made while in England, and which I propose to make again at the conference, is that even apart from these squadrons it should not be very difficult as far as possible to keep Canadians together. There is undoubtedly the feeling both in this country and beyond it, that it is to the general good to mix people from all parts of the empire. To that theory I subscribe, to a certain extent.
On the other hand, I maintain that these men in squadrons are a team, and it is easier to play on a team with men you know, men of your own kind, men from your own home town, than to -play on a team with men from another town, even though you may be the best of friends and have the greatest respect for one another. Therefore, for that reason I have been devoting a great deal of my time, considerable energy and some little argumentative ability to endeavour at least to achieve a step along the line my hon. friend has mentioned.
There are operational difficulties in the way of having a wholly integrated Canadian air force. Bombers would be attached to bomber commands. Fighters would be attached to fighter commands. Other types
would be attached to coastal commands. Army cooperation squadrons would be attached to the army.
As a matter of fact the Canadian army has Canadian squadrons attached to it for army cooperation work and, I hope, will have more as soon as it is possible to form the other squadrons provided for by the Ralston-Sinclair agreement. That agreement provided for twenty-five Canadian squadrons, in addition to the three then in existence. I was hoping to have those twenty-five squadrons well established, and then ask for more. At the moment we have twenty-two. Some of them are attached to the Canadian army and work -as army cooperation squadrons, with General McNaughton. There are many more details; there is a long history of struggle and discussion connected with this matter. I think we are on the way to where I know I want to go, and where I hope the majority of the members of this house and the people of this country want to go; that is, to make our squadrons overseas as much Canadian as possible, having regard to the difficulties of operation.

The argument presented
by my hon. friend is the argument with which I have had to contend right along. It is not all plain sailing. Certainly there is something to be said for unification of operations, if I may so put it, but this is what happens. The Americans are over there, in fewer numbers than we are. They have some kind of independent command, though they operate with the R.A.F. and, I take it, are pretty well under the general command of the R.A.F. But I should like the R.C.A.F. to have at least the same status as the Americans have. Let us say they have a bomber squadron or a bomber group of their own. I doubt very much if it would be possible for them to select their own objectives, let us say, without at least consulting the higher British command; but still they could remain together as a bomber group. As a matter of fact, what we have been aiming at as our first objective is a bomber group for Canadians. Then you can send a whole group together. Of course the objection to that is that if the

War Appropriation-Air Services
group gets into trouble, then you have a very large number of Canadian casualties, whereas, interspersed as they are now with others, the casualty list becomes less glaring. But I am hoping to attain pretty well the same status that the Americans have attained with respect to internal operations, always of course under the command of some supreme British authority with regard to operations generally. I am speaking now probably out of turn, not knowing very much about the tactical end of the matter, but I doubt if we could ever achieve a completely independent command in the sense that the Canadian army is an independent command. Our international relationships with groups, commands, and so on are so close that it would be almost impossible to have what might almost be called an independent air force, but it would be possible to have a better grouping and a greater grouping of Canadian squadrons working together.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am obliged to the minister for telling me his ambitions and his objective, and I think it is quite right that he should, after he learns what the position in Britain is, strive if possible to attain that objective, if it is possible to do so. But it would seem to me irrational that the Royal Canadian Air Force should operate on its own in Britain.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Absolutely on its own, no.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Or anything approximating that. There must be coordination of effort. I am speaking as the merest layman, knowing absolutely nothing about these matters, but my reason tells me that it would be out of the picture entirely for the Royal Canadian Air Force to operate on its own. Or the Canadian army. It is kept together as a unit of course; but when the final testing time comes, when a second front, let us say, is opened on the continent, if the Canadian army is part and parcel of the expeditionary force that goes there, it will have to be under one unified command in charge of the whole expeditionary force.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They have to be under somebody.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The minister can pursue the thought he has in his mind up to a certain point, but there he must stop. I say that with great deference, and perhaps I am making a misstatement altogether, but I am just thinking out loud.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend is right. One thing I certainly hope to achieve is more grouping of Canadians and less dispersing of Canadians all over the world, even to the 44561-152
point of filling up Royal Air Force squadrons with Canadians, if necessary. I was told of squadrons of one of our partners in the commonwealth air training plan, 90 per cent of the pilots of which were Canadians, but working in a squadron, that went by another name.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
If you do that, you do not
get the senior commands for Canadians.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is an objection. If the Canadians remained all together as an integrated unit in the Canadian air force, the chances of promotion for our men would be less than when they were spread all through the Royal Air Force, because in the Royal Air Force, spread out as it is, Canadians have chances in any number of squadrons, whereas in our own squadrons they would have chances of promotion only in the limited number of squadrons we have.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: But vice versa, if you have Royal Air Force squadrons composed 90 per cent of Canadians, you will find that the senior officers are Royal Air Force men, not Royal Canadian Air Force men.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The argument of the non-Canadians, if I may put it in that way although I do not really mean that, is that if they are not distinctly Canadians belonging to a Canadian unit, they should be looked upon as Royal Air Force and profit by the chances of promotion which come to any Royal Air Force officer. As a matter of fact, a great many of my officers argue in all sincerity that it would be detrimental to our men to form wholly Canadian units. They argue against purely Canadian units because they think our men have a better chance of promotion in British units. There are two sides to the story, but I still stick to mine.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Will this new set-up affect the advanced training of our Canadian boys in Britain?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Not at all?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
No. This is when- you get into operational squadrons, not into operational training squadrons. Of course if our force is almost an integral part of the Royal Air Force, our men, after they have served a certain time in active operations, may be put in charge of Royal Air Force operational training. As a matter of fact, after they have done a certain number of hours on operational work, they are brought back to act as instructors or put on ground work for a certain length of time in operational training.



War Appropriation

Air Services

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Then it would be better as it is, as far as the advanced training of our men is concerned?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The training is the joint air training plan as we have it in Canada, or in some cases advanced training in Britain, but that has nothing to do with the matter one way or another. We could have the advanced training here, and in all probability we shall have it here very shortly. The , only reason why we did not have it here before was that the operational types of aircraft were required urgently on the other side, and they 'did not want to send them over here but wished to keep , them over there to fight as well as to be used for training purposes. It would be a long journey for them to come over here and go back again when they were urgently required. That is why operational training units were established in Britain. That situation does not obtain to the same extent to-day, and now it will be quite possible to give operational training in Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Would the minister care to state how far our training goes in Canada, and how much training has to be given in Britain? I take it that the operational training is all given in Britain.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
That has been the case,
but it is not now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is it proposed to give more of the training in Canada, to train them here for a longer period? It would seem that if they were trained in operational work here, it would be much more advantageous, and then within a limited time after they went overseas they would be ready to go into action.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Under the joint air training plan we brought them up to a certain stage. That was part of the plan, and until very recently it was not possible to have operational training here because we could not get the operational type of planes, since they were required both for fighting and training in Britain. There is no point in sending fighting planes over here when they are needed badly over there. But that situation has eased, and there are now operational units in this country and will be many more of them here. One of the shifts, as I called it yesterday, that we are now undergoing is to enable a longer period of training to be given here, to train men in operational work so that there will be little or nothing in the way of training required when they reach overseas and have to use the biggest or fastest type of machines.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is the objective?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes, and we are on the verge of reaching it. But it could not be done earlier, and it was not part of the joint air training plan anyway.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The hon. and fair member for Edmonton East (Mrs. Casselman) last night mentioned what the women in the air force were doing in her part of the country. Would the minister be good enough to explain how the training of the women is carried on? I think the ladies would like to know that. There are over 2,600 women in the air force. Are there women medical officers on the strength who check over these ladies before they are accepted?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We are training women at Havergal college and other places. I can tell the hon. member what we are training them for, but I do not know how it is done.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Perhaps the Minister of Pensions and National Health could tell us that.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I think what the hon. member for Edmonton East was speaking of is the new system of dietitians. Diet was one of our great troubles. I am glad the Minister of National Defence is not here. I always say that you can feed foot-sloggers with pork and beans and bully beef, but the gentlemen of the air force, who really are university students during the time of their training, do not have to do the arduous physical work that the foot-slogging infantiy man has to do. Therefore we found that the ration issued by the army service corps was too heavy for these young lads, and we had to get to work to see if we could not provide them with more vitamins, or calories-I do not know which-and, particularly in the summer time, more fruits, vegetables and salads.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is proteins.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I do not know. I shall have to get some medical man to correct this when it goes into Hansard. In any event, we found that the diet was too heavy for men doing the type of work required of our personnel. We had many meetings with army officials, and finally we have reached the place where the army diet and our own are approximately the same. We came to the conclusion that we should obtain the services of the best dietitians available in Canada. We went to Eaton's, Toronto, and obtained the services of a dietitian who was being remunerated at much more than we could afford to pay to her as a serving officer in the women's division: the difference, however, has been made up by a patriotic person in Toronto. We applied to other places of this kind, and

War Appropriation-Air Services
now we have seven, or perhaps eight, women dietitians, carefully selected by Doctor Tisdale, a Toronto dietitian, and others, including Air Commodore Ryan of the medical corps. We hope the results will be not only a saving of food, but that, the food being better cooked, the quality will be improved and the health of our men will be very much better.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: In other words, you are summoning modern science to your aid.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Why not? The air is the most modern of all arms of war; why not summon the help of modem science?
To come back to positions in the Royal Canadian Air Force, women's division: clerks, equipment assistants, telephone operators, general duties, cooks, nursing orderlies, fabric workers, transport drivers-those are about all the positions which are at present available.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No technicians at all?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Technicians in the sense of mechanics and so on?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Not at present. I do not see any.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I know that in England, according to the last report received, there are only a hundred. I wondered if we had any here.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Not yet. We expect to replace 15,000 men by 15,000 women within a year or a year and a half.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Can the minister answer as regards women medical officers?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes, we have women medical officers. I cannot tell the hon. member how many.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
There are two questions I should like to ask with reference to this women's division of the air force. First, are they replacing any of the men in one of the minister's offices-I do not know how to describe them, because I resent the expression used by the minister to describe the infantry- the men who will eventually win this war as they did the last war, the "foot-sloggers"? If he wishes to use that term about the finest branch of the army, I might use one in connection with his branch in at least one part. Are any of the these females used to replace the petticoat army we have had in the Jackson building?
44561-152J

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I rather resent the expression "petticoat army we have in the Jackson building". Our men are doing a good job there.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What clothes are issued to this women's army?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We are doing a good job in the Jackson building, and I think the officers of the force there deserve great credit for the work which is being done on the empire training scheme. We are replacing a great many of the men in clerical positions in the Jackson building by women-clerks, telephone operators and others who are in the women's division.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am glad to hear that.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We propose to do that right along. As a matter of fact, on stations 136 women take the place of 126 men, as mess-women, on general duties, as telephone operators, fabric workers and transport drivers- which is not a bad average when you come to think of it-releasing men to go overseas or to lonely stations along the Pacific coast or up in Labrador, and those are jobs which are not easy for any men, even for "foot-sloggers".

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Like the hon. member for-Fraser Valley, I rather resented the expression used by the minister a few moments ago. I know, however, it was not intended to hurt.
We have been pleased indeed with the report of the minister, and I think there is every reason to believe that his branch of the service is in very good shape. Upon that, of course, the minister and all those connected with his department are to be congratulated. However, the fact that two boats have been sunk in the St. Lawrence river may indicate that considerably more needs to be done. I believe the minister himself said yesterday that he is not satisfied by any means that all had been done that could be done.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Not, that could be done; that might be done.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Our services overseas are doing well. He explained the work of our airmen who are travelling through the northern part of this dominion on patrol work.
The commonwealth air training plan, known as Canada's greatest contribution to the war so far, is also recognized as a success not only by the people of Canada but by our allies. There is no reason why it should not be a success. We have heard praise-well deserved praise-heaped on the minister here. He has been called very efficient, and I am sure we all agree. That is the first essential of a successful department. Also he is the head of

War Appropriation-Air Services
the most popular service in Canada, more popular than the navy and, certainly, than the army. He has all .the money he requires; whenever money is needed for the air force it is always forthcoming. All the men in his branch are active service men, not, as in the army, a hybrid, partly active and partly reserve. All these factors contribute to make a very satisfactory and efficient service. Men are more anxious to join the air force than any other branches of the service. One reason, possibly, is that they get more action. The minister said yesterday that the Canadian air force was the fighting force, I think, in Europe at the present time as far as Canada was concerned. That is the meaning I attached to his remark that they were doing all the fighting; I did not understand him to mean that they were doing all the fighting and that the British air force was doing none.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: He meant that they were doing all the fighting that the Canadian forces are doing apart from the navy. Well, young men like to get into the service for action. There is also the matter of the uniform; the air force uniform is more attractive to young men than is the army uniform.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It was a mistake to do away with the kilts.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: There is a Scotsman speaking. If someone would do away with his bagpipes on Saturday afternoons-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I would rather see him
have two bagpipes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The air force also have
better camps and better accommodation. The minister said a few minutes ago that they are the gentlemen's service. There is no question about that. It has been the gentlemen's service. They get everything they need, and about that I have no complaint.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
And everything they
want.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes. I heard an hon.
member say yesterday that they had cold storage for their salvage. From reports I have heard, it would be very much in keeping with the way in which they are treated.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I have an answer to that.
Our medical officer insists that the garbage be placed in cold storage; otherwise it might contaminate the surrounding area.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I do not wish to introduce any discordant note into the discussion, but there is a certain amount of discrimination. To the public every man in the air force blue 
is a hero. I do not think they realize that for one man who is up in the air there are fifteen on the ground. Is that not correct?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Twelve to fifteen.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Yes; but to the public
every man who wears the air force blue is a hero. I know of towns and other places in the dominion where there are both air force men and men in khaki, and the air force receive very different treatment from that given the men in khaki. There is great discrimination. It may be that the public should be educated in a matter of this kind, for it is most unfair. As regards the air crew, I listened with much pride yesterday to the minister and others as they detailed the exploits of our airmen. I know that in the last war it was a matter of pride for all of us to read accounts of such men as Bishop. Barker, Collishaw, McKeevor, Carter and other R.A.F. heroes; and the men in the present war are living up to the reputation then established. I was pleased to hear the minister say that we in Canada do not perhaps advertise the exploits of our heroes as much as we should. I remember Rickenbacker, the great United States airman, whose exploits certainly deserve great credit, but we have many Canadians whose deeds were just as great. In my own province we had an airman named Carter who in a few months made as good a record as did Rickenbacker. But while Rickenbacker's name is a household word in the United States, and indeed in Canada, for every school boy knows it, I doubt very much that Carter's name is known except to a few people in the community in which he lived. That is the difference. Therefore the minister's idea of advertising the exploits of our men is a particularly good one. But all men are not in the air. There are ground crews, those engaged in general duties and others, fourteen or fifteen men on the ground to one in the air.
There is one criticism I have to make in this connection. The attraction of the air force has, I believe, taken from the army men who should have remained in the army. It has been my experience that when representatives of the air force came to the training centres, and it was generally known they were there, a great many young men wished to see them. A good many of them went to the air force thinking they would be pilots or would be in the ground crew, but eventually most of them found themselves being used for general duties. I know of young men who, I believe, would have given far better service to the country had they remained as infantrymen or artillerymen, instead of, as I

War Appropriation-Air Services
heard one hon. member say yesterday, being used to wash dishes and sweep floors in messes and other places.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
In order to get my hon.
friend's opinion, as I said yesterday there is a very strong feeling that the air force should no longer go into training camps to get recruits. What does my hon. friend think?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I am rather of that opinion.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: What about the air crew? The question is being discussed, and I am asking my hon. friend for his opinion.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: In the basic training centres the district officers commanding ask that the R.C.A.F. be given every opportunity to get the men they need, and that policy was followed out. It was after they found that a great many of these men going to the R.C.A.F. were not making good, particularly as ground crew, or not having any opportunity of being in the air, that the difference came. They were retained in the R.C.A.F., but were used for menial jobs. All these men could and would have made good infantrymen and some might have been non-commissioned officer material.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We should certainly keep out of the standard duty field, should we not?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The minister said yesterday that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) and his department were getting together on that question, and I think that is something which should be carefully considered by the different departments of our services. A good many of these men become disillusioned. They have written to me stating that they were very much disappointed that they did not get the work for which they thought they were best suited. The minister yesterday referred to the question of manpower. If I understood him aright, he said they would soon run short of air crews.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Not soon.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
But there was the possibility of it. I believe he also stated that there were about 13,000 young men, graduates of high schools and colleges, who were available each year. Is there no possibility-as a matter of fact I think the minister mentioned it-of promoting young men from these ground crews and then bringing in men from the outside for their particular work. There is also the matter of the exchange of men from the army. I mentioned a moment ago that there were men in the air force who, in my opinion, should not be there, and I think there are also men in the army who would be better in the air force. If there were some
liaison along this line there could be an exchange of men to the benefit of both services.
I have a number of questions which I intended asking, but most of them have already been asked by other hon. members. Last year the minister told us that he hoped that by September, 1941, he would have twenty-five squadrons, called Canadian squadrons, in the R.A.F. I understand he has twenty-two. I have been very much interested in the debate as to whether these Canadian squadrons should be R.A.F. or should be Canadian. I appreciate the arguments which the minister has presented to us both for and against this possibility.
One thing he did not mention in that connection occurs to me. We read continually, as an almost nightly occurrence, of the Royal Air Force having made a trip over Europe. But we never read that the Royal Canadian Air Force has made a trip over Europe. subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
What is going to happen
when March, 1943, comes round.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: That is what we are having a conference for next week.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Would the minister enlighten the committee' just a little more on the division of expenses for Royal Canadian Air Force personnel and equipment outside Canada? Possibly if I had a better understanding of the agreement dealing with the commonwealth air training plan, I might not need to ask some of these questions. For instance, do we pay for all our personnel in Great Britain and the other fighting fronts, for the aeroplanes which they use and the cost of maintaining them? If not, what is the quid pro quo that we give in return? Do we give it under the air training plan? I notice in the estimates which the minister brought down, that the amount allotted for expenses overseas is relatively small compared with the total. I do not think the people of Canada have very much understanding of how much of the expense of the commonwealth air training plan is borne by the Canadian people, and how much of the expense of maintaining our boys fighting overseas is borne by us and how much by Britain. Would the minister make a general statement as to the division of expenditure?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Our headquarters overseas and our three original squadrons are paid and maintained, as to both equipment and aircraft, by us. That is Canada's direct contribution- the headquarters overseas and the three original squadrons. We pay for the aeroplanes, pay and allowances, and everything else connected with that.
With respect to the empire training plan, that is a training organization, and every graduate, from the moment he is posted overseas, belongs to the Royal Air Force. They are Royal Canadian Air Force, but they belong to the Royal Air Force. Under clause 15 which I read some time ago, the Royal Air Force pays them, and we make up the difference out of our own bounty, so to speak.

Articles 16 and 17 of the agreement read:
16.	The government of the United Kingdom will, subject to the provisions of article 17, provide the pay, allowances, pensions and other non-effective benefits, maintenance and other expenses of the pilots and aircraft crews who are trained in Canada (other than those made available for service with the Royal Canadian Air Force in accordance with the provisions of article 14) -
Those are the men who stay in Canada.
-with effect from the dates of their embarkation in Canada for service with, or in conjunction with, the Royal Air Force. The government of the United Kingdom also undertakes to arrange for those pupils who are made available for service with, or in conjunction with, the Royal Air Force, to be embarked as speedily as possible after the completion of their training, and to defray the cost of their passages to the stations to which they are appointed on leaving Canada.
17.	The pay, allowances, pensions and other non-effective benefits, maintenance and other expenses, for which the government of the United Kingdom undertakes liability under the provisions of article 16 will be as laid down in Royal Air Force regulations. If it should be decided by the government of Canada, the government of Australia, or the government of New Zealand to supplement the amounts so issued, any such supplement will be borne by the government concerned.
That is what we are doing. Our own men are paid by the Royal Air Force, and we supplement the amount with regard to the aircraft and the twenty-two squadrons. The aircraft is supplied by the United Kingdom government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Who pays for it?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: They pay for it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: How do the financial accounts really stand, if you can determine them at all? We gave a billion dollar credit to Britain recently, but now we learn that our boys who are fighting in the old country are maintained at the expense of Britain and, in some instances, paid by Britain.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Oh, yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is there any way of computing just what Britain's contribution is for maintaining and servicing Canadian fighters overseas whom we look upon as our fighters, and what is Canada's contribution? Is there any way of putting a dollar sign on Britain's contribution so that we can equate that against the billion dollar gift we have recently approved?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
All I can say is that the balance is on our side as far as the dollars are concerned. I have been trying to get the matter straightened out in my mind and in other people's minds for a long' time. Personally I think we should call the accounts

War Appropriation-Air Services
all square, say that we have spent here so much, and they have spent there so much, and let it go at that. That would be my personal view. I do not think it would hurt anybody, but of course that is unorthodox finance.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Better
keep the accounts straight.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: It will take two or three generations of accountants to untangle the snarl in which these accounts are by this time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We have stripped Great Britain of all her Canadian dollar securities, and we think we have done a grand thing by giving her a billion dollar credit, but now we find that there are offsetting factors. I am not trying to raise anything contentious at all, but I think we are entitled to know and the people of Canada are entitled to know, as far as possible, how things stand. If that cannot be done, as the minister has just indicated, we must all look upon it as a joint war in which we all are glad to do what we can.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We pay the dependents' allowances for the Royal Canadian Air Force. A pilot earns $197.50 a month, I understand, and he is paid over there. What portion of that amount is he allowed to send out of Britain to his family in Canada?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I do not know. He is paid at Royal Air Force rates. I suppose he could assign as much as he likes, but there may be some limit. I think the hon. member for Royal would know what the limit is.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The point is how much money he is allowed to send out of Britain, in view of the exchange situation.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: His British pay? I could not say.

speechtext: Last night I asked the minister whether in locating aerodromes for the air training plan any consideration was given to the possibility of their being used in a commercial air service after the war. Would the minister care to answer that question?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I do not think consideration was given to that. On two or three occasions I have read into Hansard statements indicating the factors which governed in the choice of aerodromes, and the considerations were largely military. I do not think any consideration was given to what one might call the salvage value of these aerodromes after the war.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO PUS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is it not true that the private schools to which the minister referred are strategically located so that they can be of value after the war?
